newsitem.title: USA: U.S. House votes to speed family planning funds.
newsitem.headline: U.S. House votes to speed family planning funds.

text.p: The House of Representatives voted narrowly on Thursday to free U.S. funding for international population programmes in an action some portrayed as the first test vote on abortion in the new Congress.
The House then prepared to consider a bill reinstating restrictions on overseas family planning aid imposed by Presidents Ronald Reagan and George Bush but scrapped by President Bill Clinton.

Following a replay of numerous past debates over U.S. aid for international family planning, the House approved and sent to the Senate a resolution starting to release the $385 million in aid funds on March 1. The vote was 220-209.

Under a compromise agreement last year that authorised the aid, release of the money was delayed until July 1 unless the president found the limitation was having a negative impact on population programmes, a finding that Clinton has made.
Opponents of the measure said that while the United States barred aid for abortion family planning funds would indirectly support abortion programmes by population control groups.

A separate bill sponsored by anti-abortion activist Christopher Smith, a New Jersey Republican, seeks to prevent this by reinstating the Reagan-era policy denying funds for population groups that perform or advocate abortion, even if they use their own money for that purpose. The bill would also release additional funding.

Under legislation triggered by the administration-backed resolution, monthly payouts would be limited to a maximum of 8 percent -- meaning that only $215 million of the $385 million appropriation could be spent by the end of the fiscal year. Smith's bill would remove these limits.

Secretary of State Madeleine Albright has lobbied for the resolution, telling a House panel Clinton had determined that further delay of funds "will cause a tragic rise in unintended pregnancies, abortions and maternal and child deaths."

During the House debate, Illinois Republican Henry Hyde said the issue "is not about family planning -- this is about abortion." He added: "The wall between abortion and family planning should remain in place," as it is under Smith's bill.
Smith said the administration-backed resolution "is strongly pro-abortion in its effect -- fat payday for abortion providers."
Supporters of the resolution cited exploding populations of less-developed countries leading to famine, environmental degradation and export of American jobs to low-wage countries.
"We must not hold the poor children of the world hostage to congressional politics," Representative Nancy Pelosi, a California Democrat, said.

Representative Tony Hall, an Ohio Democrat who described himself as pro-life, said anti-abortion forces had gone too far by making release of the funds a "pro-life" issue. "Pro-life forces have done great damage to poor communities all over the world."
